name: Adams, Rebecca
response: The American Civil War was caused by a complex set of factors, but slavery was at the heart of all of them. The most obvious cause was slavery itself. By the 1850s, abolitionists were gaining influence in the North, fueled by works like Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin and events like John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry in 1859. The South's entire economy was built on enslaved labor, making abolition an existential threat. The second major cause was the political crisis over westward expansion. Every new territory reignited the slavery debate — the Missouri Compromise of 1820, the Compromise of 1850, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 all tried to settle the question but only deepened divisions. The Kansas-Nebraska Act led to 'Bleeding Kansas' and destroyed the Whig Party, giving rise to the Republicans. These causes were deeply interconnected: states' rights arguments were really about the right to own slaves. Economic differences between North and South stemmed from the South's reliance on enslaved labor. Political compromises kept failing because slavery was a moral issue that couldn't be split down the middle. I believe slavery was the most significant cause because every other tension — states' rights, economics, territorial disputes — ultimately traced back to whether humans could be property. Lincoln's 1860 election, on a platform opposing slavery's expansion, triggered secession precisely because the South saw any threat to slavery as a threat to its existence. While other factors created conditions for war, without slavery they likely would have been resolved politically.

name: Brooks, William
response: The Civil War had multiple causes but slavery was the central issue that connected them all. First, the moral and economic reality of slavery created an irreconcilable divide. The South depended on enslaved labor for cotton production, which was the backbone of its economy. Meanwhile, the abolitionist movement grew stronger in the North, especially after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 forced Northerners to participate in returning escaped enslaved people. Second, the question of whether slavery would expand into new territories created constant political crises. The Missouri Compromise, Compromise of 1850, and Kansas-Nebraska Act were all failed attempts to manage this tension. The Dred Scott decision of 1857, in which the Supreme Court ruled that enslaved people were not citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in territories, made compromise nearly impossible. These causes fed into each other — territorial expansion was really about expanding slavery, and states' rights arguments were fundamentally about states' rights to permit slavery. Economic differences between the industrial North and agrarian South were rooted in the South's slave-based agricultural system. I argue slavery was the most significant cause because it was the issue that made compromise impossible. Other democracies resolved economic and political tensions without civil war, but the moral dimension of slavery made it uniquely intractable. That said, the political failures of the 1850s — particularly the collapse of the Whig Party and the rise of sectional parties — accelerated the path to war.

name: Campbell, Jasmine
response: The two biggest causes of the Civil War were slavery and states' rights. Slavery was the major issue because the South needed slaves for their cotton plantations and the North wanted to end it. The Missouri Compromise and Kansas-Nebraska Act tried to balance slave and free states but it didn't work. States' rights was also important because Southern states believed they had the right to make their own decisions about slavery without the federal government telling them what to do. These two issues were connected because the states' rights debate was really about whether states could keep slavery. I think slavery was the most important cause because that's what all the fighting was really about. Even the election of Lincoln caused the South to leave because they were afraid he would end slavery.

name: Davis, Michael
response: There were several causes of the Civil War. Slavery was one cause because the North and South disagreed about it. States' rights was another cause because Southern states wanted more power. Economic differences also played a role because the North had factories and the South had farms. These things were all connected because they made the North and South different from each other. I think slavery was the most important cause.

name: Ellis, Hannah
response: The Civil War was primarily caused by the institution of slavery and the political failures surrounding it. Slavery created a deep moral divide — the abolitionist movement, strengthened by figures like Frederick Douglass and events like the publication of Uncle Tom's Cabin, challenged the South's entire way of life. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made the conflict personal for Northerners who were now legally required to assist in capturing runaways. The territorial question was equally explosive. The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 overturned the Missouri Compromise and introduced popular sovereignty, leading to violent conflict in Kansas. This political instability destroyed existing political parties and created the sectional Republican Party. These causes were inseparable. The economic argument — that the North was industrial while the South was agricultural — only existed because Southern agriculture relied on enslaved labor. States' rights rhetoric was deployed specifically to protect slavery, as evidenced by the fact that Southern states had no problem with federal power when it enforced the Fugitive Slave Act. I believe slavery was the most significant cause, but I recognize it was the political system's inability to resolve the slavery question that ultimately led to war. The Dred Scott decision, Bleeding Kansas, and Lincoln's election were all political flashpoints that made compromise impossible.

name: Ivanova, Katya
response: The Civil War was caused by slavery and economic differences between North and South. The North had an industrial economy and didn't need slaves, while the South had a farming economy that depended on slave labor for cotton. These issues were connected because the economic system in the South was built on slavery. The Missouri Compromise and other laws tried to keep peace but failed. Slavery was the most important cause because everything else came from it.

name: Johnson, Derek
response: Two major causes of the Civil War were the debate over slavery's expansion into western territories and the breakdown of political compromise. The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 was a turning point — by allowing popular sovereignty in new territories, it effectively repealed the Missouri Compromise and led to violent conflict in Kansas between pro-slavery and anti-slavery settlers. The Dred Scott decision of 1857 further inflamed tensions when the Supreme Court ruled that Congress had no authority to ban slavery in territories. These causes were interconnected because the territorial debate was fundamentally about slavery's future. As the nation expanded, each new state threatened to tip the balance of power in Congress. The failure of political institutions to manage this tension — the collapse of the Whig Party, the rise of the Republicans, and the fracturing of the Democrats — made war increasingly likely. I believe the failure of political compromise was the most significant proximate cause, even though slavery was the underlying issue. The Constitution had been designed to manage sectional differences, but by the 1850s the system broke down. However, I acknowledge that slavery was the root cause that made all these political failures so dangerous.

name: Klein, Rachel

name: Lee, Nathan

When new states were added, there was always a fight about whether they'd be slave or free states. The Missouri Compromise and Compromise of 1850 tried to fix this but they were just temporary. These two causes were connected because the fight over territories was really a fight about spreading slavery. I think slavery was the biggest cause because it was the issue that nobody could compromise on.

name: Newman, Grace
response: The Civil War had two main causes: slavery and political polarization. Slavery divided the nation morally and economically. The South's plantation system depended entirely on enslaved labor, and events like the Nat Turner rebellion (1831) and the growth of the abolitionist movement created deep fear in the South about losing their labor system. The Fugitive Slave Act required Northern cooperation in returning escaped people, which actually increased Northern opposition to slavery. Political polarization was the second cause. The two-party system that had managed sectional tensions broke down in the 1850s. The Kansas-Nebraska Act split the Democratic Party along sectional lines and the Whig Party collapsed entirely. The new Republican Party was entirely Northern, meaning there was no longer a national party that could bridge the divide. These causes reinforced each other. Political polarization made it impossible to compromise on slavery, and the slavery debate drove the polarization. I think slavery was the primary cause because political systems can usually manage disagreements — but slavery was a moral issue where 'compromise' meant accepting that some humans were property. Even Lincoln, who initially promised not to interfere with slavery where it existed, was seen as an existential threat simply because he opposed its expansion.

name: Park, Jennifer
response: There were many causes of the Civil War. Slavery was the main one. The South wanted to keep slaves because their economy depended on it. The North wanted to end slavery. They also disagreed about states' rights and whether the federal government could tell states what to do. The Missouri Compromise tried to balance slave states and free states. I think slavery was the most important cause because that's what they were mainly fighting about.

name: Quinn, Ethan
response: The causes of the Civil War were slavery, states rights, and economics. They were all connected. Slavery was the most important.

name: Ramirez, Lucia
response: The Civil War resulted from the intersection of slavery, territorial expansion, and political failure. Slavery was the root cause — it created irreconcilable moral, economic, and social divisions. The South's cotton economy generated enormous wealth through enslaved labor, and slaveholders held disproportionate political power through the Three-Fifths Compromise. The abolitionist movement, led by figures like Frederick Douglass and William Lloyd Garrison, challenged this system morally and politically. Territorial expansion brought the crisis to a head. The Louisiana Purchase, Mexican-American War, and subsequent territorial acquisitions forced repeated confrontations. The Missouri Compromise (1820) drew a geographic line, but the Compromise of 1850 and especially the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) shattered this framework. The resulting violence in Kansas and the rise of the Republican Party showed that democratic institutions were failing to contain the conflict. These factors were deeply interconnected. Southern states' rights arguments were deployed specifically to protect slavery — the same states that championed states' rights enthusiastically supported the federal Fugitive Slave Act when it served their interests. Economic differences between regions existed because of slavery. Political failures occurred because slavery was an issue where genuine compromise was morally impossible. I argue slavery was the most significant cause, and the historical evidence overwhelmingly supports this. The declarations of secession from Southern states explicitly cited the preservation of slavery as their primary motivation. Mississippi's declaration stated: 'Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery — the greatest material interest of the world.' While other factors contributed to the timing and nature of the conflict, slavery was the necessary and sufficient cause without which war would not have occurred.

name: Sullivan, Emma
response: Two causes of the Civil War were slavery and economic differences. The South had plantations and needed slaves. The North had factories. The Missouri Compromise tried to keep things balanced. These issues were connected because the Southern economy depended on slavery. I believe slavery was the most important cause because it affected everything else about the disagreement between North and South.
